# `html/element-permitted-content`

**Elements contain only content HTML allows there**

| | |
|---|---|
| **Pack** | `@codelaw/rules-html` (npm) · `codelaw-rules-html` (PyPI) |
| **Languages** | HTML |
| **Turned on by** | `codelaw:html/recommended` at `error` |
| **Severity when named without one** | `error` |
| **Options** | none — severity only |
| **Fix** | `manual` — no automatic fix; the steps are under *How to fix* (the right structure depends on what the markup is for) |
| **Stability** | `preview` — runs only with `preview = true` |
| **Since** | 0.1.0 |
| **Ported from** | `html-validate/element-permitted-content` |

## What it checks

Each element contains only the elements its content model allows: no `<div>` inside a `<span>` or `<p>`, nothing interactive inside a link or button, no `<li>` directly inside a `<div>`.

**Why:** Browsers repair forbidden nesting by moving elements, so the DOM differs from the markup and styles and scripts miss.

## Configuration

Everything below goes in `codelaw.toml` at the repo root. The same keys work as `[tool.codelaw]` in `pyproject.toml` or `"codelaw"` in `package.json` ([SR-CONFIG](../../../records/0110_config.md)).

### Turn it on

**Install the pack** (`codelaw init` does it for the languages it finds):

```bash
npm install --save-dev @codelaw/rules-html
pip install codelaw-rules-html
```

**Then extend a preset that turns it on** — `codelaw:html/recommended` sets it to `error`:

```toml
preview = true                        # pack rules are preview today
extends = ["codelaw:html/recommended"]
```

- **A rule exists only once its pack is loaded** through `extends`; naming it in `[rules]` without that is an unknown rule id (exit 2).
- **Without `preview = true`** the rule is skipped and codelaw warns that it is preview.

### Severity

```toml
[rules]
"html/element-permitted-content" = "warn"    # error | warn | info | off
```

- **`error`** fails the run (exit 1) · **`warn`** fails only with `--max-warnings N` · **`info`** never fails · **`off`** turns it off.
- **Naming it with a severity turns it on** even when no preset does.

### For a group of files

A `[scope.<name>]` gives some files their own setting, applied after `[rules]` — a scope of your own needs `files`:

```toml
[scope.legacy]
files = ["src/legacy/**/*.html"]
rules = { "html/element-permitted-content" = "off" }
```

A scope's `remap` changes whole severities in its files, after everything else: `remap = { error = "warn" }` never fails the run there.

### Warn locally, fail in CI

The `ci` profile runs when `CI` is set; `local` otherwise; `--profile <name>` or `CODELAW_PROFILE` picks one.

```toml
[profile.local.rules]
"html/element-permitted-content" = "warn"

[profile.ci.rules]
"html/element-permitted-content" = "error"
```

### In `pyproject.toml` or `package.json`

```toml
# pyproject.toml
[tool.codelaw.rules]
"html/element-permitted-content" = { severity = "warn" }
```

```json
{
  "codelaw": {
    "rules": {
      "html/element-permitted-content": {"severity": "warn"}
    }
  }
}
```

### Silence one finding

An inline `codelaw-ignore` always needs a reason; `expires=`, `warn_days=` and `by=` date it ([SR-LINTER](../../../records/0106_linter.md) decision 6).

- **HTML:** `<!-- codelaw-ignore html/element-permitted-content: <reason> -->`
- **Dated:** `<!-- codelaw-ignore html/element-permitted-content expires=2026-12-31 by=you@example.com: <reason> -->`

### Keep today's findings, fail on new ones

```bash
codelaw baseline add --rule html/element-permitted-content --expires 2026-12-31 --reason "<why>"
```

See [SR-BASELINE](../../../records/0104_baseline-and-deprecations.md).

### See what applies

```bash
codelaw explain html/element-permitted-content       # what it wants, why, how to fix
codelaw check --rule html/element-permitted-content  # only this rule
codelaw config --print --for <file>                  # the resolved setting, and where it came from
```

## How to fix

1. Move the element named in the message out of the parent it can't be in.
2. Or change the parent to one that allows it (for example `<div>` instead of `<span>`).

## Examples

### HTML

#### Don't

```html
<p><div>Block</div></p>
<a href="/a"><button type="button">Go</button></a>
```

#### Do

```html
<div><p>Block</p></div>
<a href="/a">Go</a>
```

## Differences from the source

Obsolete elements (`<tt>`, `<font>`, `<acronym>`, …) have no content model in the element table, so html-validate reports them wherever they are; here they are left to `html/deprecated`, which reports each once.
